clue.text: Horny beast and colonist run off together

parts.note: ants live in colonies, so an ant is a colonist
lovers who elope run off together to marry

explanation.surface: A horned animal and a settler running away as a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonist' sounds like a settler, but it is an insect that lives in a colony.
explanation.definitionFit: An antelope is a hoofed grazing animal, most species of which carry horns.

clue.text: Big Brother writer has cast actor for second half

indicators.note: the actor letters stand in for the latter half of the writer word, so only its first half is kept

parts.note: a writer is an author

indicators.note: cast in the sense of thrown about, so the letters of actor are reshaped

explanation.surface: Orwell, Big Brother's creator, assigns a performer to the second half of something.
explanation.walkthrough: AUTHOR loses its second half, HOR, and 'cast' rearranges ACTOR to OCRAT in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Brother, from Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, is the archetypal all-controlling dictator.

clue.text: Reporter's still writing material?

indicators.note: a reporter speaks the news, so what follows is a word as it is heard

parts.note: still means stationary, not moving

explanation.surface: A journalist's equipment is still paper and pens.
explanation.walkthrough: STATIONARY (not moving) and STATIONERY (paper goods) are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationery covers paper, envelopes and pens, the supplies used for writing.

clue.text: Boring way to describe Reading?

definitions.meaning: bland and unadventurous, appealing to the average taste
a whimsical literal reading: Reading, an English town, sits along the old main road west out of London

explanation.surface: A dull way of describing the Berkshire town of Reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading is a large town in Berkshire, west of London on the old Bath Road; the second reading takes the phrase literally as a location.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-of-the-road describes anything safe and moderate that avoids extremes, hence dull.

clue.text: Look to oust broadcaster's central position in syndicate

indicators.note: to oust means to force out, so one letter is driven off and replaced
the letter in the central position of the broadcaster's initials is the one removed

parts.note: the BBC is Britain's public broadcaster
lo is an old word meaning look!

explanation.surface: An invitation to see someone displace a broadcaster's central role in a consortium.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle B of BBC gives way to LO, leaving B-LO-C.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of nations or parties combining for a common purpose, as a syndicate does.

clue.text: Word used by unprincipled genius

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A term favoured by a clever but unscrupulous person.
explanation.definitionFit: To give your word is to make a solemn promise, which is a pledge.

clue.text: Publicist dashes round entrance outside court

indicators.note: turned round, so the letters of the dashes word run backwards

parts.note: to nip is to dash somewhere quickly

indicators.note: the entrance word stands outside the court abbreviation, enclosing it

parts.note: a door is an entrance

explanation.surface: A PR person rushes around a doorway outside a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: Nip in the British sense of popping out quickly gives 'dashes'; 'round' reverses it, and 'outside' wraps the entrance around the court abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin doctor is a press agent who presents news in the most favourable light.

clue.text: River Test perhaps associated with certain types of plant

definitions.text: associated with certain types of plant

parts.note: the Indus is a great river of Pakistan
a test is an example of a trial

explanation.surface: The Hampshire river Test is linked with particular plant species.
explanation.walkthrough: The River Test is a famous English chalk stream, which is what the surface wants; here 'River' and 'Test' work separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial plant means factory machinery, so industrial relates to that kind of plant rather than flora.

clue.text: See 1
Where one might go to mix and produce New Order

definitions.meaning: a place people go to for holidays
to ... is to jumble things and arrange them in a new order

explanation.surface: A venue for socialising and making music like the band New Order.
explanation.walkthrough: New Order is a Manchester band, but here the words just mean a fresh arrangement: re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort is a holiday destination, and as a verb re-sort means sorting again.

clue.text: Effete English rogue gripped by depression

indicators.note: held tightly inside, so the depression word wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: a dent is a depression in a surface
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue

explanation.surface: A weak Englishman, a scoundrel, sunk in gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' suggests low mood, but it is a physical dent.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete and decadent both suggest self-indulgent weakness and moral decline.

clue.text: Person who employs American head of state

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, was the British monarch and head of state

explanation.surface: An employer who is the US President.
explanation.definitionFit: A user is someone who makes use of, or employs, something.

clue.text: Part of fence catching small rider in Grand National lottery?

indicators.note: the fence part holds the other pieces as if caught inside it

parts.note: a stake is a post forming part of a fence
wee is Scottish for small
a rider is an addition to a document, as a PS is

explanation.surface: A jockey caught in a jump at the Grand National, Britain's famous steeplechase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rider' suggests a jockey, but it is a postscript. The Grand National is a British horse race on which office sweepstakes are traditional.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweepstake is a betting pool where drawn horses decide the winner, a lottery on a race.

clue.text: Explicit film stopping progress by one member going too far

parts.note: overt means open and explicit

indicators.note: stopping as in plugging a gap, so the film fills the middle of the other word

parts.note: to hop is to move along on one leg
ET is the Spielberg film

explanation.surface: A graphic film halting the advance of one politician who is overreaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' suggests an MP, but it is a leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the top is an idiom for excessive or exaggerated behaviour.

clue.text: American tortoise jumped into water to get bird

parts.note: Americans commonly call tortoises turtles
dove is the American past tense of dive

explanation.surface: A US tortoise plunges into a pond to catch a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The turtle dove is a small wild pigeon with a purring call.

clue.text: Where Force acts also leads to violence and vandalism

definitions.meaning: the point at which the pull of weight on a body effectively acts
the middle letter of gravity, V, is the leading letter of both violence and vandalism

explanation.surface: Wherever police act, it also provokes violence and vandalism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' looks like the police; it is the physical force of gravity. The second part describes V, the central letter of GRAVITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics treats a body's weight as acting at one point, its centre of gravity.

clue.text: Characterful piece given alternative title, oddly

indicators.note: an alternative form of the word given is a rearrangement of its letters
oddly picks the letters in odd positions, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: A piece of character writing offered under another title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' reshapes GIVEN to VIGNE; 'oddly' takes T, T, E from TITLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A vignette is a brief evocative sketch, often a character study.

clue.text: Approach case of leprosy with treatment of dubious validity

indicators.note: treatment as in processing, so the letters are worked into a new order
the case of a word is its outside, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Tackling leprosy with a remedy that may not work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' looks medical but rearranges APPROACH plus LY, the outside of 'leprosy'.
explanation.definitionFit: An apocryphal story is widely told but probably untrue, so of doubtful authenticity.

clue.text: Damp and sticky like shellfish?

definitions.meaning: ... describes unpleasantly moist skin or air
read playfully as clam-y, resembling clams

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented sense 'like a clam'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clammy means moist and cold, as sweaty hands feel.

clue.text: Show embarrassment, ultimately going pink

indicators.note: the ultimate letter goes, so the phrase is cut short at its end

parts.note: to go red is to blush with embarrassment

explanation.surface: Blushing, finally turning pink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pink' looks like the colour but is the old verb meaning to pierce or stab.
explanation.definitionFit: To pink is to prick or wound with a pointed weapon, as a bull's horn would.

clue.text: Relatively unknown economist ran German banks

indicators.note: banks as in keeps safe inside, so the words hold the answer within them

explanation.surface: An obscure economist was running German banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' suggests finance but signals the letters held across 'economist ran German'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stranger as a comparative adjective means more unfamiliar, so comparatively little known.

clue.text: Struggle to breathe when doctor rings

indicators.note: rings as in encircles, so the doctor goes round the other piece

parts.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
as can mean when

explanation.surface: Breathless while a physician telephones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rings' suggests a phone call, but means surrounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To gasp is to take sharp, laboured breaths.

clue.text: Dull parent replaces contents of diary

indicators.note: the inner letters of the diary word are swapped out for the new piece

parts.note: to parent a child is to rear it

explanation.surface: A boring mother or father rewrites what's in a journal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parent' looks like a noun but is the verb rear.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary and dull both mean depressingly uninteresting.

clue.text: Core component deleted from Android's top-level directory

indicators.note: the central letter of the android word is the one taken out

parts.note: an android is a robot

explanation.surface: A key file removed from an Android phone's main folder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Android' suggests the phone system but is a humanoid machine.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing the root is the highest directory in a file system's hierarchy.

clue.text: Glance through second novel by Kipling

parts.note: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's novel

explanation.surface: Briefly look over another Kipling novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' looks like 'another' but is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: To skim a text is to read it quickly and superficially.

clue.text: Where fare-dodger's journey ends?

parts.note: fare means food as well as a ticket price, so one who dodges all food ends in a fatal state that contains a railway stop

explanation.surface: Where a ticketless passenger gets off.
explanation.walkthrough: A fare-dodger evades the train fare; read 'fare' as food, and the end of refusing it is starving, a word ending in -ATION like a STATION stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who avoids all food eventually suffers fatal hunger, a pun on train stop.
